Kiss
KISS
n., v.
Old English cyssan. Webster 1828: to salute with the lips; a salutation given with the lips, in token of affection or reverence. In Scripture the kiss is a public sign — of family affection, of covenant loyalty, of submission to a king, and, once, of the most famous treachery in history.

Biblical Definition

A kiss in Scripture is a formal sign given in public, not a private sentiment. Isaac calls Jacob near: Come near now, and kiss me, my son (Genesis 27:26), and it is the kiss that accompanies the blessing. Laban complains that Jacob fled and did not let him kiss my sons and my daughters (Genesis 31:28). Solomon makes it the reward of honest speech: Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer (Proverbs 24:26). Above all it is the sign of submission to a king, which is why the second psalm ends the way it does: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him (Psalm 2:12). The nations that were raging are commanded to do homage. The New Testament makes the kiss the ordinary greeting of the congregation: Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you (Romans 16:16). And it records the counterfeit. Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him and killed him (2 Samuel 20:9). Judas agreed a sign in advance (Matthew 26:48), and our Lord named it as he gave it: Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KISS as a salute given with the lips, in token of affection, respect or reverence; and notes the ancient custom of kissing as an act of homage and of religious veneration.

expand to see more

KISS, n. — A salute given with the lips; a common token of affection.

KISS, v.t. — To salute with the lips. To treat with fondness; to caress.

In ancient usage the kiss was also an act of homage or subjection rendered to a superior, and an act of religious veneration paid to idols — as in 1 Kings 19:18, of those who have not kissed Baal.

Webster’s note on homage is the key to Psalm 2:12. The command to kiss the Son is not an invitation to feel warmly toward Him; it is the demand that rebel kings submit.

Key Scripture

Genesis 27:26 — "And his father Isaac said unto him, Come near now, and kiss me, my son."

Psalm 2:12 — "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him."

Proverbs 24:26 — "Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer."

Luke 22:48 — "But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?"

Romans 16:16 — "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 2:12 is corrupted when the kiss is read as devotional warmth rather than as the homage of a subject — which turns a command to rebel rulers into a private feeling, and empties the psalm of its politics.

expand to see more

The second psalm is addressed to kings and judges of the earth who are taking counsel against the LORD and against His anointed, and its conclusion is an ultimatum: Be wise now therefore, O ye kings… Kiss the Son, lest he be angry. The kiss commanded is the ancient gesture of a vassal to his sovereign. Read as an invitation to affectionate feeling, the psalm loses its argument, and with it the doctrine of the mediatorial kingship of Christ over the nations — that the risen Lord holds actual authority over states and rulers now, and not merely over private hearts. That doctrine is the ground of the Christian’s duty to the magistrate and of the magistrate’s duty to Christ, and it is why the Reformers preached this psalm to princes.

The counterfeit kiss is the second warning and it is aimed at the church. Joab’s greeting and Judas’s sign both used the outward form of covenant affection to accomplish betrayal, and our Lord’s question — betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? — names the perversion exactly. Paul’s holy kiss is the redeemed form: a public greeting among people who genuinely belong to one another. The adjective is doing the work. A congregation with warm greetings and cold conduct has the form Judas used, and the letters that command the holy kiss also command that love be without dissimulation (Romans 12:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew nashaq means to kiss and also to arm or equip, a homonym the Old Testament exploits; the Greek philema is the noun, and kataphileo, to kiss fervently, is what Judas did.

expand to see more

Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to kiss; also, in a related form, to be armed or equipped, which is why some render Psalm 2:12 with the idea of doing homage.

Hebrew nashaq in 1 Kings 19:18 — the seven thousand which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him; the kiss as idolatrous homage.

Greek philema (G5370) — a kiss; the holy kiss of Romans 16:16, 1 Corinthians 16:20, and 1 Thessalonians 5:26.

Greek kataphileo (G2705) — to kiss fervently or repeatedly; used of Judas in Matthew 26:49 and of the woman at our Lord’s feet in Luke 7:38.

The Aramaic-influenced text of Psalm 2:12 has generated debate over Kiss the Son; the KJV’s rendering follows the reading the church has read messianically from the beginning, and Acts 4:25-26 quotes the psalm of Christ.

Usage

"Kiss the Son, lest he be angry (Psalm 2:12) — homage demanded of rulers, not affection invited from individuals."

"Betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48) — the sign of covenant loyalty used as the sign of betrayal."

"Salute one another with an holy kiss (Romans 16:16) — the ordinary greeting of a congregation, and the adjective is not decorative."
